claim: Christianity Today published 'How Great Is Our Claude' by Kelsey Kramer McGinnis on October 2, 2026, about AI tools worship leaders built to build setlists and score songs.
quote: Worship leaders have built new AI tools to help create setlists and score songs on qualities like scriptural grounding and clarity.

claim: SongTheology was designed by worship leader Tyler Anson Newberry; he wrote the grid language and the tool uses Claude to analyze lyrics pulled from Google.
quote: He wrote the language for the grid, and the tool relies on the AI tool Claude to perform the analysis of lyrics (pulled from Google) and provide theological feedback.

claim: SongTheology scores songs out of 35 across seven categories.
quote: see its score out of 35 possible points, given according to the strength of the lyrics in each of Newberry’s seven categories: “scriptural grounding,” “doctrinal clarity,” “God-centeredness,” “gospel presence,” “clarity vs. ambiguity,” “congregational usefulness,” and “pastoral durability.”

claim: Each category is scored 1-5; totals of 30-35 mean 'use freely' and below 18 'probably avoid'.
quote: 30 – 35 Strong · Use freely 24 – 29 Good · Use thoughtfully 18 – 23 Use with caution Below 18 Probably avoid

claim: SongTheology evaluates lyrics only, irrespective of artist or church affiliation.
quote: This tool evaluates lyrics only, irrespective of artist or church affiliation.

claim: The God-Centeredness category asks whether the song's center of gravity is God or the singer's own experience.
quote: Where is the center of gravity: God’s character and works, or mainly my experience of God?

claim: The Pastoral Durability category asks whether a suffering person can sing the song honestly.
quote: Can someone suffering sing it honestly? Does it make room for waiting, weakness, repentance, or unanswered prayer?

claim: SongTheology also lets worship leaders score original lyrics and says it does not store them.
quote: We do not save or store your lyrics in any way. They’re used only to generate this score, then discarded.

claim: Example: 'Gratitude' by Brandon Lake scored 20 of 35 with flags for gospel clarity and emotion without theological grounding.
quote: the popular song “Gratitude” by Brandon Lake scores 20 out of 35, with two criticisms (“flags”) for its lack of “gospel clarity” and “emotion without theological grounding.”

claim: 'Come, Thou Fount of Every Blessing' is the most-searched song on SongTheology.
quote: “Come, Thou Fount of Every Blessing” is the most-searched song.

claim: Newberry says many young worship leaders lack a theological grid for evaluating songs.
quote: “A lot of younger worship leaders don’t have a mental theology grid for the worship songs they encounter.”

claim: Newberry and his wife Leslianne left full-time church ministry just over a year ago to start the nonprofit Asaph's Table.
quote: Just over a year ago, Newberry and his wife, Leslianne Newberry, left full-time church ministry to start Asaph’s Table, a nonprofit that offers support and training to worship leaders

claim: Asaph's Table describes itself as a registered 501(c)(3) nonprofit caring for worship leaders.
quote: Asaph’s Table is a registered 501(c)(3) nonprofit.

claim: Newberry frames SongTheology as a training aid meant to make itself unnecessary.
quote: It’s a tool to help you begin to not need this tool.

claim: Asaph, founded by worship leader Alex Moyse, tracks the emotional and theological balance of a church's worship sets over time.
quote: Rather than individually evaluating songs, Asaph is designed to track and evaluate the emotional and theological balance of a church’s worship sets over time.

claim: Asaph also relies on Claude.
quote: Like SongTheology, Asaph relies on Claude.

claim: Asaph markets gap analysis of underused themes, theological gaps and overused emotions.
quote: Import your library and get instant analysis of underused themes, gaps in theology or overused emotions.

claim: Asaph syncs with Planning Center via a Chrome extension; Planning Center is optional.
quote: Nope! Upload your songs via CSV and start planning. PCO integration is optional.

claim: Asaph's homepage claims 900+ worship leaders and a 10,000+ song database.
quote: Join 900+ worship leaders planning with Asaph

claim: Asaph's About page gives a lower user figure of 300+ worship leaders (inconsistent with homepage).
quote: We're actively serving 300+ worship leaders

claim: Asaph says it does not dictate songs and that the leader always has final say.
quote: AI gives you a starting point—you always have final say. Edit, replace, or reorder anything.

claim: Asaph says technology cannot replace a pastoral heart but can give back time.
quote: Technology can't replace your pastoral heart. But it can give you back time. For prayer. For your family. For your team.

claim: Moyse says his team uses Claude in a limited way with a human in the loop.
quote: It’s doing a lot of the grunt work, and there is still a human in the loop.

claim: Moyse says AI is not trained to think about worship theology on its own.
quote: “AI is not trained to think about this stuff,” Moyse said.

claim: Neither tool is endorsed by a denomination or tradition; both founders wrote their own criteria and use Claude to apply them.
quote: Both Newberry and Moyse say they have created their own evaluation criteria and are using Claude to apply them. Neither tool is endorsed by a particular denomination or tradition.

claim: Researcher Mark Porter tested Asaph and found it can build a coherent set, while questioning whether it prompts reflection.
quote: “It can put together a coherent musical set,” said Porter. “I think anything that pushes people to be more reflective about the selection of music can be a good thing. But there’s the question ‘Does this tool do that?’”

claim: Porter warns the tools must not shortcut a leader's own reflection.
quote: “You can’t use it to shortcut your own reflection and engagement,” said Porter.

claim: Porter says lyric-only analysis misses meanings songs acquire over time.
quote: Over time, they acquire meanings and uses that aren’t captured in the text.

claim: Porter notes the instructions builders give the AI reflect their own point of view.
quote: The people using AI to build these tools also have a point of view that informs the instructions they are giving the technology.

claim: Mark Porter holds a doctorate in ethnomusicology and has served as a church worship leader and organist.
quote: Mark is a musician who has served as worship leader, director of music, organist and choir leader for a variety of churches

claim: A Reformed Worship essay (Benjamin P. Snoek, July 2026) cites Asaph's repertoire reports as a possible insightful starting point.
quote: which uses AI to suggest emotional contours through a congregation’s song repertoire, can be an insightful starting point for considering how sung prayers balance

claim: The same essay warns against using AI to shortcut the priestly work of worship leaders.
quote: There is a problem, though, when we leverage technology to shortcut, not support, the priestly work incumbent on worship leaders.

claim: The ELCA released a theological foundation paper, 'Artificial Intelligence (AI) and ELCA Social Teaching'; it is not new social teaching.
quote: does not represent new social teaching, it does outline ethical concerns surrounding the transformational technology

claim: The ELCA paper is six pages and called the beginning of a conversation; ethicists plan to explore AI further in January 2027.
quote: The paper is not the ELCA’s final teaching but rather the beginning of a conversation, as Lutheran ethicists plan to explore AI further at the group’s meeting in January 2027.

claim: The ELCA paper calls AI 'a breathtaking means' of human innovation that may promote well-being.
quote: AI is one means, a breathtaking means, of humanity’s power to innovate in ways that may promote the well-being of creation and human society.

claim: The ELCA paper says every AI application should include accountable humans in the loop.
quote: every application of AI includes human beings in the loop who remain accountable for its use

claim: The ELCA paper names reduced human capacity for critical thinking as a danger of AI.
quote: Such dangers inherent to the use of AI include displacement of workers and the potential reduction in human capacity for critical thinking.

claim: The ELCA paper respects the consciences of members on both sides of AI use.
quote: this church recognizes the need to respect the consciences of Lutherans faithfully wrestling with the ethics of AI

claim: The ELCA paper opens with the Golden Rule (Matthew 7:12) as its frame.
quote: “In everything do to others as you would have them do to you; for this is the Law and the Prophets.” -- Matthew 7:12
